title: The Educated Barbarian: An introduction to Stoicism (Enchiridion analysis part 2)
summary: Second Enchiridion episode: illness cannot touch the will, and temperance, endurance and patience apply to training and life. He covers minimalism over possessions, ignoring others' opinions, keeping the ego and shadow in check, the social Stoic, and disagrees with Epictetus on fate.
claims: Disease impedes the body but not the will; its real damage is the mind syncing with the diminished body. He knew people who died of minor illnesses because their weakness kept them from recovering
Many mental health issues are biological, but treating them as unable to impede your will makes you a tougher adversary for them
The will chooses and nothing is pushed on you; always keep your agency strong because it is always yours
An insult needs your permission to hurt; brushing it off saves energy, denies the aggressor the reaction and shows them temperance
Temperance in training means knowing when enough is enough: a certain intensity is needed, then you retreat
He felt something pop in his leg dodging a car on his bike, still went to the gym conservatively, warmed up on deadlifts, did his working sets, and the pain disappeared
Take every safe opportunity to show endurance and do not let small inconveniences stop your training
Patience is the key virtue: do not train intensely for two weeks then quit; stick to it and hard work tells no lies
Owning more made him anxious and greedy (he kept shoes he would not wear); realizing it pushed him to a minimalist life that feels freer
You take nothing to the grave; what remains is the help and impact you had on others
Do not shape your behavior around others' opinions; a low-value pack pulls you down, so build your own intrinsic sense of value
Be confident and tell yourself you are right in the moment; you can always change your mind later
Be intelligent rather than spending your effort trying to appear intelligent
If people regard you as important, distrust yourself: authority feeds the ego, you listen to sycophants and lose touch with reason
Make friends with your shadow (Jung) rather than trying to kill it; know your limits, drives and vices to keep them in check
The Stoic is a social creature and exemplary citizen, not a lone wolf; a country of Stoics would be incredibly powerful
He disagrees with Epictetus that your role is assigned by God: free will prevails, you can change your part, and taking credit for that change is better for the soul
Whatever part you currently have, do not whine; play it as well as you can while working to change it
